activities.name: mbtQuestionMatch

config.prompt: Five tools, five different questions — pair them:
config.why: The toolkit chains in exactly that order in a real experiment: amplify, check, read — then edit.

activities.caption: fill the blanks — the two facts under the toolkit
activities.name: mbtRawCloze

config.text: DNA's sugar-phosphate backbone carries a %%0%% charge on every phosphate, which makes it movable by electric fields. Its two strands separate when heated near %%1%% °C and re-anneal by base pairing: A–T with %%2%% hydrogen bonds, G–C with %%3%%.
config.hint: Charge makes DNA sortable; reversible strand separation makes it copyable — every technique here uses one or both.

activities.caption: call the magnitude — the gene count
activities.name: mbtGenesEstimate

config.prompt: One human cell folds about 3.1 billion base pairs into a 6 μm nucleus. Roughly how many of those letters code for proteins — i.e. how many protein-coding genes are sprinkled through the genome?
config.why: ~20,000 protein-coding genes; the rest is regulatory sequence, introns, repeats and history — which is why finding one specific 200-letter stretch is a one-in-ten-million search.
config.context: PCR finds the needle by exponentially copying only the needle; profiling reduces three billion letters to twenty informative numbers.

activities.anchor: Insulin was the first mass product
activities.caption: rebuild the recombinant-DNA recipe
activities.name: mbtCloneOrder

config.prompt: From human gene to bacterial factory, 1972–73 style — put the recipe in order:
items: Cut the plasmid and the human insert with the same restriction enzyme
The staggered cuts leave matching single-stranded sticky ends
Return the construct to a bacterium
The bacterium copies the construct for free
Human insulin from bacterial fermentation — the first mass product, 1982
config.why: Scissors with addressable targets (EcoRI reads GAATTC, cutting between G and A), sticky ends that anneal, ligase to seal, and a free copying machine — that pair of facts founded recombinant DNA.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — the thermal-cycle answer
activities.name: mbtTaqSpot

config.prompt: This PCR answer contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Each cycle runs three temperatures: ~95 °C, then ~50–60 °C, then ~72 °C.
At ~95 °C the double helix denatures into single strands.
At ~50–60 °C the synthetic primers anneal to the two strands flanking the target.
At ~72 °C the polymerase extends the primers along the template.
Taq polymerase is destroyed by the 95 °C step, so a fresh batch must be added by hand after every cycle.
A thermal cycler automates the temperature dance — 30 cycles in about 90 minutes.
config.correction: Taq polymerase SURVIVES the denaturation step — that heat stability is what made thermal cycling automatic.
config.why: Taq comes from the hot-spring bacterium Thermus aquaticus; it rides out 95 °C, so the tubes just go into the thermal cycler — no hand-adding between cycles.

activities.caption: file the PCR variants by what they read
activities.name: mbtVariantBuckets

config.prompt: Three PCR variants, three specialities. File each fact:

items.label: the RT-PCR tests that ran the COVID-19 pandemic
reads the starting amount from the cycle number at threshold
Ct below 30 means a high viral load
one constant temperature, no heating/cooling dance

config.why: Reverse-transcription PCR makes RNA viruses readable, quantitative PCR reads amounts from Ct values, and isothermal methods trade the thermal cycler for the field.

activities.anchor: every fragment migrates toward the positive electrode
activities.caption: bet first — which fragment wins the gel race?
activities.name: mbtGelPredict

config.q: Two DNA fragments start at the same well: 200 bp and 2,000 bp. Which reaches the far end of the gel first?
choices: The 2,000 bp one — the field pulls on its larger negative charge
They arrive together — both have the same charge-to-mass ratio
The 200 bp one — it threads the gel's polymer mesh more easily
config.why: Force and inertia scale together: every fragment has the same charge-to-mass ratio, so the extra pull on the long one is cancelled by its extra mass. Separation comes only from threading the mesh — small runs fast, large lag, roughly logarithmically in length.

activities.anchor: the cell's choice, and it is the designer's lever
activities.caption: run the CRISPR repair decision
activities.name: mbtCrisprBranch

config.root: Your ~20-letter guide RNA has paired with its genomic target, and Cas9 has cut both strands — provided the PAM licence check passed. The break now sits in a living cell's hands.

start.text: Cas9 has cut. You control the repair conditions — what do you supply?

choices.label: A repair template with the sequence you want
choices.feedback: Precise HDR editing — the template is what gets written in.

choices.label: Nothing — let the cell's sloppy repair handle it
choices.feedback: NHEJ disrupts the gene: a knockout.

choices.label: Cut again, to be sure
choices.feedback: Guides have off-target cuts — every extra cut adds risk.

hdr.text: Precise HDR editing done — reading has become writing. Applications stack: disease-resistant crops without foreign DNA, base- and prime-editing that cut less.

nhej.text: A knockout. That lever is exactly what Casgevy (2023, sickle-cell) pulls — knocking out a repressor to reactivate fetal haemoglobin.

off.text: The craft is designing the controls that expose error bars — one clean cut beats several uncertain ones.

config.why: Sloppy NHEJ repair knocks genes out; a supplied template channels precise HDR. The ethical line since the 2018 He Jiankui case: somatic therapy yes with oversight, heritable germline editing no — for now.
